blocks.text: Jeremiah 49:7-16 and Obadiah 1-8 share extensive wording in their declarations against Edom. The overlap itself is clear, but its origin is disputed: Jeremiah may have drawn from Obadiah, Obadiah may have drawn from Jeremiah, both may reuse a common tradition, or later editorial work may have combined inherited material. Terms such as quotation, source, shared anthem, and common tradition therefore describe competing explanations rather than settled facts.

Jeremiah 49 belongs to the collection of declarations concerning nations in chapters 46-51. More broadly, the received book combines poetry, prose sermons, narratives, letters, headings, repeated accounts, restoration collections, nation oracles, and an appendix, reflecting a long and disputed compositional history. The Masoretic and Old Greek forms preserve markedly different ancient editions: the Old Greek form is roughly one-seventh shorter and places the nation oracles earlier and in a different order. These differences caution against assuming that Jeremiah’s present arrangement was its only ancient form.
